facts.text: Pakrek Stair-builder, the old miller of the Gate Mill, died at Crownsgate.

At the reading after Pakrek Stair-builder's death, his son Giktrok Spear-thrower, an under-clerk of the crown sealing office, laid down a will sealed at Highcrossing that leaves him the Gate Mill, against the village grant that names his cousin Kemed Oath-keeper its miller.

Crown clerks out of the sealing office at Highcrossing have called a 'sealing tenth' on every crown-sealed grant along the Crossing and Marches roads, owed by midsummer in coin, grain or men; holders who cannot pay are taken into bond-service in the emperor's new company.

Laʻetalu of the Bark-Field House, lord of Oathford, has marched the emperor's new company up the wall road and quartered it in Longwall's empty outer towers by the Throne's leave, and the company's riders now stop every cart on the Crossing and march roads to take the sealing tenth by force.

The crown has re-granted the tolls of the Great Bridge at Southroad to the emperor's new company under a fresh seal, over the head of the lord who built it; the Silver Road Counting-House has advanced the company a year's pay against those tolls; and crown coin is buying Southroad's toll-keepers one by one.

At Litiṭaʻa of the Great House's word, an imperial writ read out in the Empty Gallery and nailed up in every Great House town names Kemed Oath-keeper a forger of crown seals: no sealing office, market court or archive is to take a paper from her hand, and whoever shelters her answers for it.

The emperor's new company has seized Crownsgate for the crown 'from a forger's kin', taken the Gate Mill and the village's winter grain into crown keeping, and holds the village's grant-holders in the old gate-house until they swear their grants to the crown; and by a proclamation read in every Great House town the Throne has named the company the emperor's own guard.

Litiṭaʻa of the Great House is raising the emperor's new company to hold Highcrossing for the Throne when her brother dies, before Haʻahoqo the General can count Longwall's soldiers as his own. She pays for it by re-granting mills, fords and tolls to crown-bound holders under papers she seals herself in Gahìru's name, because his hands can no longer hold the seal; the will that took the Gate Mill was the first paper she sealed so.
Trerxuq Fire-walker, a crown clerk out of Highcrossing, carried Giktrok Spear-thrower's will to Crownsgate and lodged in the crown gate-house the week of the reading.
The seal-proofs Trerxuq Fire-walker sold at Crownsgate and the will that claims the Gate Mill carry the same new crown seal, pressed in the sealing office at Highcrossing.
The tenth's coin and its bondsmen go to the emperor's new company, which Laʻetalu of the Bark-Field House, lord of Oathford, is raising in the Throne's pay.
Xipid Road-warden, who drove the Gate Mill's wagon, struck the company's sergeant at Bogford ford and was carried off to the lord's tower at Oathford under the crown clerk's warrant.
At the Last Well the tenth-clerk read out the Road Crews' haulage contract with the crown as the paper the crews' tenth is owed on.

Ḍuhuḍì of the Spring-Cliff House, the old crown gate-warden at Crownsgate, refused to open the crown gate to the company's riders without the emperor's own hand on the order, and says the seal they carried is not his.
Haʻahoqo the General will stand with Kemed Oath-keeper against the emperor's new company, if the company's arms and the bondsmen's oaths come to Longwall once it is broken.
The carts that go round by the quiet ways say the company's riders come out of Longwall's outer towers every dawn, and that the towers were opened to them from inside.
Hiqìṭuḍe of the Rain-Hollow House opened the outer towers on Laʻetalu of the Bark-Field House's word that he came as the emperor's own captain.
The carts that went round by the Reed Crossing are stranded under the Brennock road fort, and riders out of the Reedbank camp have begun to strike them at night.
Among the stranded carts hides Nuqug Wall-warden, a bondsman who deserted the company, and he says he will tell what he saw at Highcrossing to whoever gets him to Breakwall.
Thelohoʻu of the Herb-Field House's father, the old toll-keeper Tasho of the Herb-Field House, keeps a paper from the bridge's building in the west toll hut, and doesn't know what it is.
Tasho says the Great Bridge's toll-gate chain-post was sound at dusk on the night before the crown's re-grant was read on the bridge.
Giktrok Spear-thrower, the under-clerk who claimed the Gate Mill, has been turned out of the sealing office and hides with the drovers on the river meadows.
Giktrok says Trerxuq Fire-walker has pledged the Gate Mill's grain to the Counting-House against the company's pay, and goes to the Scales Hall himself on quarter-day.
Writ-riders took Gurile of the Tree-Ledge House, Dorì's ferry-lad, who had hidden Kemed in his boat, and rode up the Elderhollow road.
The riders meant to sell word of Kemed's road to the head of Elderhollow's ruling house, who has sworn to bar her at the town's bridge.
The writ's papers came to Nami of the Rain Bay from Fewash of the Old Road, a Saltmarket notary selling 'clearances' to those the writ names.
Fewash's clearances are stamped at the crown factor's stall on the Unchained Quay at Openharbour.
With the company's columns held sick at Oathford, the grant-holders it took at Crownsgate are kept in the old gate-house under a short guard.
Aheh of the Silk Road says the company's captain made the grant-holders swear to the Throne's keeper by name, not to the emperor.
Shasauthu of the Silk Road says the company's clerks still read Kemed's name out as a forger at every muster.

The will is not the old miller's. Giktrok Spear-thrower put his father's name to it at Trerxuq Fire-walker's word, to clear what he owed the clerk; Ḍuhuḍì of the Spring-Cliff House sat with Pakrek Stair-builder in his last month and heard him promise the mill to Kemed.
Aheh of the Silk Road gathered his neighbours' silver for the seal-proofs himself, and kept a tenth of it for his trouble.
Trerxuq Fire-walker sold eleven of Crownsgate's grant-holders 'seal-proofs' at three silver each, to guard their grants against claims like the Gate Mill's, and took the silver back to Highcrossing.

When the company's riders came to Bogford ford for the Gate Mill's tenth, the sergeant Lawinuu of the Reed Cove took the mill's flour wagon and its oxen in place of the coin, and Hausethayai of the Quiet Road took them as his share for letting the crown's clerks work his land.
Hausethayai of the Quiet Road has already promised the wagon and its oxen to the overseer of the bond-field below Bogford, to haul for the slave-bought field.
Xipid Road-warden did strike Lawinuu of the Reed Cove at Bogford ford, hard enough to break his jaw, when the sergeant cut the oxen from the wagon's traces.
Doqoṭuḍì of the Grass-Ledge House did fire the crown's tally-shed at Bogford ford when the clerks took his team, with the tenth-clerk's boy asleep in its loft; the boy lived, burned.

The haulage contract in the Long Shed's strongbox, in the old foreman's hand, says the crown pays each load on delivery and owes the crews' road no tenth; the crews stopped hauling only after a season's pay went missing.
The crown's haulage chest is empty: the sealing office has been paying old loads with new tenths.
Doruḍoqu the Carter has called the Road Crews to vote in the Long Shed on striking against the Counting-House's rates.
The trade road moved: since the company's riders took the Crossing road, the carts of three lordships go round by the Reed Crossing, and no one passes the Broken Shrine's stalls.
Hiqìṭuḍe of the Rain-Hollow House, warden of Longwall's outer towers, opened them to the emperor's new company.
The veterans had a hand in it: they stopped keeping the outer towers' watch when the pay stopped at midwinter, and left the warden alone on the wall with the keys.
The commission Laʻetalu of the Bark-Field House carries is a fair copy; the sealed original lies in Litiṭaʻa of the Great House's own rooms at Highcrossing, behind the Empty Gallery.

The causeway was built badly for this: laid for mules and smugglers' handcarts, a plank wide on reed bundles, it was never meant to bear loaded wagons, and every wagon since midsummer has sunk it further.
The Reedbank band was driven out of its old ground in the bog camps when the company's riders swept the march road for bondsmen.
Dortik First-striker, a carter among the stranded, has been selling the Reedbank riders word of which carts carry the tenth-coin, to see the crown's silver taken.
Texar Ore-finder, who keeps the Reed Crossing, sold Laʻetalu's riders word of which road the deserter would take.

Shahayuh of the South Road and Litiṭaʻa of the Great House have sworn before Southroad's ladder-keeper that a champions' bout at the tavern-yard ring decides who holds the Great Bridge's toll-house until the court hears his appeal.
Yiheyaeh of the East Road has bet the company's own silver on the crown's champion at long odds, and means to pay the company's arrears from the winnings.
The founding grant is what it looks like: Gahìru of the Great House's grant of the bridge-right to Shahayuh of the South Road, sealed by the emperor's own hand in the year the bridge was raised.

Ruqred Iron-breaker, the company's sapper, drew the toll-gate's chain-post in the night on Yiheyaeh of the East Road's word, so the gate would fall on Ḍoʻiqiʻi of the Ember-Ledge House, the toll-reeve who would not take crown coin; it fell on Dodìli of the Thorn-Hollow House's cart instead.
The Great Bridge's toll-gate came down at first light and crushed Dodìli of the Thorn-Hollow House's cart, and her leg with it.
Each claim holds in part: the meadows' old grant gives the crown their grass in a time of muster, and the drovers have grazed them by custom for sixty years without one.

Giktrok carries a leaf torn from the sealing office's day-book, the page for the day his father's will was sealed, sewn into his coat; it is why the clerks turned him out, and why he will not be taken anywhere the sealing office can find him.
Nuihina of the Blue Reef, the Counting-House clerk who wrote the pledge, saw Trerxuq Fire-walker sign the Gate Mill's grain over to the house in his own name, and has told no one.

Trerxuq Fire-walker, Giktrok's master at the sealing office, swore the Gate Mill would be his, then pledged its grain to the Counting-House against the company's pay and had him turned out of the office.

Giqo of the Vine-Cliff House told the company's clerk that his mother had carried Kemed's letters about the crown seals over the ford for a season; the writ cites those letters, read in her own hand, as its proof, and she has not spoken to him since.
Thahuh of the Wind Road has carried Oathford's ford since Dorì was shunned for a forger's letters, and the longer mother and son stay apart, the longer the company's custom is his.

The band already has a better buyer for Gurile than any writ reward: the overseer of Hausethayai of the Quiet Road's bond-field will pay for a strong young ferry-lad, and the band means to move him there before the new moon.
Thahuh of the Wind Road sold word of Kemed's road to Roduhuli of the Three-Ring House, whose house bars her at Elderhollow's bridge.
When the writ was read, Trerxuq Fire-walker took every paper from Kemed's hand at Crownsgate, the village grant among them, and the sealing office sold the forger's papers off as scrap vellum.

The grant Nami of the Rain Bay holds is Crownsgate's own copy; the original, sealed when the village gave Kemed the mill, was sent to the Ninth Ring's archive for keeping, as every crown village's grants are.
Ponor Far-seer, the notary's apprentice, copied the clearances from a letter in Laʻetalu of the Bark-Field House's hand, and has told no one.
Fewash sells the clearances on Laʻetalu of the Bark-Field House's orders, and the silver goes to the company's chest.

Fewash of the Old Road sold 'clearances' of the writ to salt-carters, ferrymen and lodging-keepers who had carried for Kemed, at a month's wage each; the writ's officers tore them up at the first gate.
On the Unchained Quay, before the market crowd, Kemed Oath-keeper called the crown factor Weyeh of the Hill Road's seals forgeries pressed in another's name.
Nothing settles what Kemed said on the quay: the crowd's tellings disagree, and the market clerk who wrote the day's quarrels lost the page to the tide.
The cough came in with the remounts Numeleo of the Kelp Pool sold the company out of the Marches, bought cheap from a bog farm where it had already killed half a herd.
The tenth is real and fair: every Crownsgate grant was a crown grant with a tenth written into its seal-clause, and none of them has paid it in forty years.
The wrong is as Xipid tells it: the writ that named his sister a forger, and the seizure that took her mill as a forger's goods, were both sealed at Litiṭaʻa of the Great House's word.
Litiṭaʻa of the Great House had Kemed Oath-keeper named a forger by imperial writ, and her mill seized as a forger's kin's.
Shasauthu carries the crown's tenth-roll of every oath Crownsgate swore, taken from the muster clerk's chest the night he decided to come home; it is why he won't be seen on the road.
The stain is false and was made so on purpose, off this card: Litiṭaʻa of the Great House had the writ sealed against Kemed because hers was the hand setting the new seals beside the old.

Laʻetalu of the Bark-Field House holds Crownsgate and the Gate Mill for the crown on the strength of 'a forger's kin'; the longer the stain stays on Kemed, the longer his company's hold on the village stands.
The inner ditch is cut too low: it runs under the mill-stream's bed and drains the stream into the ditch, as anyone can see who walks the cut at dusk.
Eheheya of the High Road asked the veterans for the ditch herself, to keep the company's riders out of the wall-village.
Eheheya can put a cart through Longwall's inner gate unasked, and the veterans on it will carry word down the crown road to Highcrossing's lower town.
Kotqot Wall-breaker's gate seized the company's tally-cart at the breach for Breakwall's wall-toll, unpaid, and holds its tally under his seal until the toll is paid.
The tally in Breakwall's strongroom is the fair copy for the paymaster at Longwall; the tenth-clerk on the march road kept the original, with every carter's mark on it.
The tally names the company's paymaster, Yiheyaeh of the East Road, on every line: his own mark shows where the tenth-coin went.
When Thahuh of the Wind Road took Oathford's ford, he shook hands with the ford-wardens on the ferry stair: their men and toll-boxes cross free, and the ford is his.
No one wrote the handshake down: the ford-wardens' clerk was at the muster that day, and the stair keeps no book.
Qahituḍe of the Moon-Ledge House will tell you which remount lines came in from the Marches, and when.
Crownsgate's households have got used to Shawasus of the Dawn Road's flatbread off the Highcrossing carts: it is cheaper than the oven's loaves, and they don't mean to go back.

The tenth-roll is wrong: it names Feiwahe of the West Road for the crown-sealed field of his neighbour Ṭuḍiqahu of the Moon-Cliff House; his own field is held by an old Free Lords' grant that owes the crown no tenth.
It is as Ritder says: her father sold the grant to pay the sealing tenth, at a tenth of its worth, and the broker simply won't sell it back.
Mokpur means to burn the old grant, so the field can be re-sealed under the crown and sold to a buyer from the Chainmarket's pens.
Huliro of the Moon-Brow House, who carts her sacks, sells the tenth-post word of which loads are hers.
Tonod told his captain which quiet roads his brother's carts used, to win his place in the company; the riders took his brother's cart on the first of them.
Wuwesh of the Rain Road, the inn's pot-boy, took the box from the stable loft while the carters slept off the wait; it is under the inn's ash-pit.
The fight is for what Tortopox says: the ox the riders took at the roadside, and the right to say so to a rider's face.
Ḍuʻa of the Bark-Crag House is bonded into the company; if she loses a challenge in its coat, her bond is doubled.
Dorog Coin-counter has called in Limawu of the Rain Stack's notes a season early and taken his crew's wagons against them.
Limawu had already missed two quarter-days on the notes; the house was within its terms, only early.
Ṭeqatiqe carries the toll-house's takings-book, with every keeper's crown coin written in it; that's why the toll-man follows, not the coin she refused.
Ini wants off the ladder: his crew boss takes his purses for the bridge's tolls, and he would sooner lose cleanly and be struck off than keep fighting for them.
The old seal-cutter's will survives in the copy-book of Longwall's tithe-house, in the tithe-clerk's hand, and leaves the shop to Ḍoʻiḍole.
Wehu of the Deep Shore sealed the bales in the market-seal house until a court rules on them: they came in on a flour-ticket written in the writ-named miller's hand.
It is as the weaver says: the bales are hers, and only the ticket is the trouble.
Wehu wants the bales gone: they fill half his seal house, and he can't release them without a ruling no court will make.
Limu of the Deep Mouth named Kotxuq Sand-walker to the writ's officers as one who had sheltered the forger, for their reward; the lodging-keeper died of cold in their cell before he was heard.
Limu is still at it: he has named two more households on the Vale road since, and the officers pay him for every one.
When the company was named the emperor's own guard, the old palace levies were turned out of Highcrossing's barracks unpaid; this band took to the roads, and has come as far as Firststone.
Pokik Hound-hunter, Gexem's own son, rides with the levies, and showed them where the farms keep their stores.
Wasiwihu of the Long Road, a wharf tallyman, has been shorting the crown's grain-sacks as they come off the boats; Menput caught him at it, and he pushed the porter off the wharf's end.
Hononaha lies about the stores: the old guard bought them with crown coin, not from its own purse, and the yard's tally-board shows it.

faces.despite_you: Though the Gate Mill's claim was settled for Kemed Oath-keeper, the sealing office says every crown-sealed grant on the roads now owes its tenth, the Gate Mill's with the rest.

faces.despite_you: Though the Long Shed held the crews' contract good and the carter from Crownsgate walked out of the lord's tower, the company now takes the tenth at the roadside, contract or no contract.
Though the Scales Hall heard the crown clerk answer for his pledge, Litiṭaʻa of the Great House had the writ read in the Empty Gallery before the news could reach the court.

Though Kemed Oath-keeper came home cleared by the Ninth Ring's archive or the Open Council's court, the company took Crownsgate 'from a forger's kin' all the same, under the Throne's writ, not theirs.

return_variants.won: Crownsgate is free of the company and the writ is torn up: the Return is the village learning to trust its miller again, with the lieutenant still holding what grants he can.
return_variants.let go: The heart gave the Gate Mill to the crown for the writ: she comes home a free woman with no mill, and the Return is her name, not her stones.
return_variants.lost: The company still holds Crownsgate and the writ stands: the Return is a homecoming under guard, the heart's name read out at every muster.
